title: Wavefront scheduling effect on PP/TP latency
content:
Purpose:
Quick lab notes and results from the "wavefront" scheduling experiments — i.e., intentionally shifting the start times of pipeline stages across replicas to change when inter-stage collectives and TP allreduces coincide on the interconnect. Goal is to determine whether small deterministic offsets reduce link contention and p95/p99 latency for small requests without hurting throughput.

Context / why we ran this:
- Production traces show rare but sharp tail spikes when many short requests with small contexts (~64 tokens) hit the cluster simultaneously.
- Hypothesis: when PP stage boundaries line up across replicas, TP collectives (allreduce/allgather of attention KV or gradient-like tensors for TP inference) create short bursts that saturate NVLink/NIC links.
- Prior experiments looked at macro-variance of interconnect (see related notes) but didn't isolate scheduling offsets between PP stages. This is a lighter-weight mitigation than rearchitecting sharding.

Experiment design:
- Hardware: 8x A100 80GB per node, NVLink mesh (full-mesh within node), PCIe to host for multi-node. Test both single-node (NVLink-only) and 2-node (NVLink+IB) scenarios.
- Model: Llama-7B equivalent topology compiled into TP=4, PP=2 layout (4-way tensor parallel, 2 pipeline stages) and also TP=8, PP=1 (TP-only) for control.
- Workload: synthetic micro-batches that emulate our short-request trace: batch_size=1, request_token_len=64, generation<=16. Arrival patterns: Poisson (base), synchronized bursts (N requests arriving within same 10ms window).
- Variables: stage_offset in microseconds between the start of stage 0 and stage 1 on each replica (0, 250us, 500us, 1ms, 2ms). Also random jitter added in some runs (uniform +/- 100us).
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99/99.9 latency per request generation (end-to-end), tail per-token time, per-stage stall time (from runtime traces), NCCL timeline contention (nvprof/nsys timeline), host->device staging read throughput.
- Commands used (local harness):
  run_wavefront_bench.py --tp 4 --pp 2 --microbatch 1 --stagger 0 --arrival burst --dur 600s 
  run_wavefront_bench.py --tp 4 --pp 2 --microbatch 1 --stagger 500us --arrival burst --dur 600s
  (harness injects stage start offsets via runtime env REDWOOD_PP_STAGE_OFFSET_US=... and a shim in the exec loop)

Key observations (single-node NVLink):
- Baseline (stagger=0): p95 = 142ms, p99 = 282ms, p999 ~ 490ms (burst arrival).
- stagger=250us: p95 = 125ms (-12%), p99 = 220ms (-22%), p999 = 360ms (-26%).
- stagger=500us: p95 = 118ms (-17%), p99 = 200ms (-29%), p999 = 330ms (-33%).
- stagger=1ms: p95 drifted a bit lower (115ms) but throughput jitter increased; marginal improvement vs 500us.
- adding random jitter (+/-100us) on top of 500us stagger improved p999 slightly (320ms) and reduced worst-case pathological alignment runs.

NCCL / timeline evidence:
- nsys timelines show that with stagger=0 many TP allreduces across replicas started within a 100us window, causing serialized packet bursts on the NVLink fabric. This corresponded to host scheduling queues spiking and GPU DMA engine saturation windows.
- With stagger=500us the allreduce starts were spread across several hundred microseconds and link utilization flattened (less instantaneous peak), seen as reduced queue depth and less overlap on the NVLink lanes.
- NIC (IB) forwarding in the 2-node case still showed microbursts, but node-local NVLink smoothing helped reduce the end-to-end effect.

Multi-node (2-node) results highlights:
- Baseline (0 offset) p99 was worse vs single-node: ~360ms.
- Staggering 500us reduced p99 to ~250ms (≈30% improvement). However, cross-node IB microbursts were still the limiting factor for p999; we saw sequence-level retransmits and small RDMA retries (increasing completion latency variance).
- Tuning: enabling NCCL_LL_THRESHOLD and increasing NCCL_NTHREADS had minor effects; the most impactful knob was staggering + enabling host staging (read-ahead of KV cache into pinned host buffers) so the PCIe window didn't coincide with an inter-node burst.

Unanticipated/interesting micro-observations:
- For TP-only runs (PP=1), small staggers still helped tail latency, suggesting benefit not only from desyncing PP barriers but from deserializing collective start times across replicas generally.
- Very large staggers (>5ms) can hurt latency because they add serialization to critical path (requests wait idle for downstream stage). So there is an optimal sweet spot ~200-800us for our setup.
- When we artificially increased microbatch size to 4 (more batching), the stagger benefit mostly disappeared — batching changes per-token work and the allreduce durations so overlap is naturally larger and smoothing is inherent.

Profiling notes / how we measured stalls:
- Runtime traces instrumented with timestamped span for: stage_start, call_tp_allreduce_start, call_tp_allreduce_end, send_to_next_stage, recv_from_prev_stage, kv_prefetch_start, kv_prefetch_end. These were pulled into a small analysis script to compute per-stage stall durations and correlation against NCCL timeline spikes.
- Used nsys for GPU timelines and tcpdump + ibdiagex snapshots for IB retransmit analysis (2-node).

Quick checklist of mitigations tried and effect:
- Staggered stage start (deterministic offsets): good, low-effort, 15-35% tail improvement typical. Need tuning per topology.
- Add small random jitter: further reduces rare pathological alignments, low cost.
- Host staging prefetch of KV cache: useful for multi-node, reduces PCIe contention windows.
- NCCL tuning (LLThreshold, buffer sizes): minor wins, not a full fix.
- Request-side admission control / windowing (shaping bursts at the router): strong effect but higher system complexity; in many cases combining stagger + light admission control gave best SLO compliance.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How stable is the sweet spot across machines with different NVSwitch/mesh wiring? Need to run on at least two different rack topologies. (Action: Marcus to arrange cluster reservations with alternate cabling, JIRA-RT-1142).
- Can the scheduler derive offsets automatically from simple telemetry (per-stage median start time) instead of static config? Propose an adaptive controller prototype in runtime. (Action: Aisha prototyping, RFC soon).
- Need to evaluate CPU overhead and request jitter when we add random jitter + stagger on fleets — is there extra jitter introduced to regular steady-state hits?
- Explore combining stagger with small intentional microbatch coalescing windows at ingress to further smooth collectives.

Next steps / proposed tactical plan (short term):
1) Add config flag REDWOOD_PP_STAGE_OFFSET_US to runtime with per-deployment default 500us and jitter +/-100us. Test on canary pool for 2 weeks (owner: Elliot).
2) Marcus: schedule follow-up runs on alternate topology (different NVSwitch wiring) and collect the same metrics.
3) Aisha: prototype a lightweight adaptive controller to nudge offsets based on observed per-stage spike alignment (data collection RFC by 2025-03-24).
4) Engineering: small tracing patch to push per-request stage_start markers into the centralized trace so we can automatically compute alignment histograms across replicas (PR link above).

Notes to future reader:
- These experiments are low-risk to ship as a runtime default (small stagger + tiny jitter) but require monitoring. Failure modes are mainly slight throughput regression on already-batched workloads.
- If anything looks off in canary we should be able to toggle off via runtime feature flag per-pool.

Raw numbers (repro snapshot):
- single-node bursts: baseline p95=142ms, p99=282ms, p999=490ms; stagger=500us -> p95=118ms, p99=200ms, p999=330ms.
- two-node bursts: baseline p99=360ms; stagger=500us -> p99=250ms; p999 ~ 480ms -> 390ms (still noisy).

Attachments / traces referenced: nsys traces uploaded to artifact store (artifact://wavefront/nsys/2025-02-20/node1/), small span logs in S3 (s3://rwd-inference-wavefront/logs/2025-02-20/).

If you want the raw harness and exact run commands, see the PR above (github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/732) — includes scripts and a synthetic trace generator that reproduces the bursts.

-- Elliot

(Notes: informal lab doc; some results depend on model micro-architecture and host PCIe bandwidth. Please ping authors if you replicate or hit different numbers.)
